The 6 Best Latte Machines for Automatic Espresso Drinks (2026)

📅 23 Aug 2018 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A latte is rich and milky heaven.
  • According to recent reports, some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop.
  • It has been revealed that most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A latte is rich and milky heaven. A cappuccino is the cloud that heaven rests on. The best latte machines and the best automatic espresso machines are the ones that can give you this richness consistently, easily, and deliciously. Home espresso machines, like the classic devices in our guide to the Best Espresso Machines, often have a reputation for being intimidating. But they don't have to be.

According to recent reports, some machines make it easy and keep you from having to drive to the coffee shop. The automatic espresso machines in this guide can make a perfect frothy cappuccino accessible with the press of a single button, or maybe a couple of buttons. Our top high-end superautomatic espresso machine, the De'Longhi Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends), is a paragon of easy-peasy, frothy, pleasing cappuccinos and flat whites. The newly introduced Ninja Cafe Luxe Pro (see here on Amazon) seems determined to produce every kind of coffee in existence.

It has been revealed that most of the machines on this list also come with grinders, but our guide to The Best Coffee Grinders may also be helpful. For more WIRED coffee coverage, check out our guides to The Best Coffee Subscriptions, The Best Drip Coffee Machines, The Best Milk Frothers, and The Best Cold Brew Makers, or look for our recent coffee gear reviews.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on WIRED UK’s blind taste test of popular fully automatic bean-to-cup machines and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

A sophisticated bean-to-cup machine from Italian coffee titan De'Longhi, the Rivelia (7/10, WIRED Recommends) immediately ranks among the most modern, impressive, user-friendly, and capable superautomatic espresso machines I’ve encountered—the sort that has you dump a half-bag of beans into a hopper and will grind, brew, then froth up milk for a flat white, amid 18 options on espresso, latte, cappuccino, and iced-coffee drink options.

Recent findings suggest that pretty much everything operates via an easy touchscreen, including bean guidance that lets you optimize the machine for each bean. The milk frother works at the press of a button and makes actual microfoam—and the foam’s density can be adjusted to make a frothier cappuccino or dense flat white. It’s so easy I let my parents test-drive it, and they fell in love with it within a day. If you’ve got multiple people using the machine, you can save multiple profiles and your favorite custom drinks. So Dad can have his basic “coffee” that’s actually a European-style café crema, and Mom can have her ridiculously large 16-ounce travel-mug latte. (Yes, these are their drinks.).

In a recent development, what's better, the Rivelia has two swappable bean hoppers, so it’s easy to swap between caff and decaf, or between light and dark roasts. Honestly, this is the bean-to-cup espresso machine that fully sold me on the idea of automatic coffee machines like this one. Though note: Fully automatic espresso machines like the Rivelia grind a little coarser, in order to make espresso less finicky and less difficult. This leads to a smoother but less nuanced profile than espresso shots you’d find in a café. But if you're a milk lover, the absolute ease with which the Rivelia froths a cappuccino will likely balance this out. The cold espresso is also a pleasant option when mixed with milk or vodka.

It has been revealed that A lot of machines can make you a cloudy, clumpy, big-bubble cappuccino without much hassle. But it's that well-integrated microfoam, the silkiness, that feels like an actual luxury—elevates a good foamed milk from the merely milky latte to silly morning ecstasy.

It has been revealed that there's a lot to like about Ninja's flagship entry into the espresso market: in particular, dosing by weight and an easy bean guidance function that actually helps in dialing in a bean. Quite simply, this machine offers real-deal, unpressurized portafilter espresso without the fussiness. But what I especially like about this Ninja is the milk. Some superautomatic machines have tube-filled, plasticky milk systems that are annoying to clean. Some never get a fine froth. This Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro is the best of each world, a steam wand and stainless steel steamer cup with a spinning whisk at its bottom that simulates the whirlpool created by a skilled barista. Whether cold foam or hot foam, Ninja's Luxe Cafe series offers truly excellent foam for your morning cup.

Sources indicate that now, for this: It is not a superautomatic machine like the Rivelia, though it’s among the easiest portafilter machines I've ever used. The conical burr grinder is built in, it doses accurately, the tamper handle is easy, and bean guidance will tell you what to do without much fuss. Mostly, you just need to transfer the portafilter from one spot on the machine to another.

Note that for a lower price, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier (described below) offers the same great milk froth, but you lose the automatic tamper and a hot water spout. For me, the Pro is the pick for a more pleasant morning and greater versatility. Note that while the massive drip tray does hold a lot of water, it’s a bit of a production to empty and replace, and that while it also purports to be a drip coffee maker, it’s nothing to write your mother about.

This Mr. Coffee machine was once our top pick for lattes. Why? Because it sits so nicely at a comfortable intersection where ease of use meets automation and affordability. This is about the lowest-priced machine you can ever expect to find with automatic milk frothing at the press of a single button, with options for latte foam or cappuccino froth. Just load fine-ground coffee into the portafilter, tamp it down, and twist it on. The machine will mix up a cappuccino or a latte macchiato at the press of a button.

This machine has a forgiving (but not overly intense or nuanced) pressurized portafilter, which means it will work with almost any “espresso-grind” coffee from your local café or the grocery store. Just note you’ll still get a better shot of espresso if you buy a grinder and use fresh beans from a good specialty roaster. But all in all, this is about the easiest $200 latte machine we know. Like, the hardest thing about it is that the milk canister can be removed and stored in the fridge, and you have to clean it out once a week.

It has been revealed that the Cafe Affetto is one of the few fully automatic machines that WIRED has enjoyed in this price range. The Affetto features a built-in steaming wand, produces 20 bars of pump pressure to ensure your espresso is fully extracted, and is a slick little machine. It’s very slim and fits comfortably on a small apartment countertop without having to rearrange everything. Because coffee production is automated, you just need to fill the water tank and put whole beans in the hopper, and you’re good to go. You can brew one or two shots with just the press of a button, and there’s a programmable button to create your favorite drinks (like an Americano with just the right amount of water).

It has been revealed that the milk frother does a lot of the work on its own. Just pour some of your favorite milk into the frothing pitcher, submerge the wand, and hit the steam button. If you’re latest to frothing milk, you don't even need to move the pitcher to produce a creamy and consistent microfoam. WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey tested the frother with dairy milk, oat milk, and soy milk, and found it produced soft and creamy café-grade froth each time. Just make sure it’s topped up with water and beans and that you clean out the spent grounds container regularly, and it works like a dream.

The Breville Oracle Jet (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is my favorite of the two dozen or so fresh espresso machines I’ve tried so far this year. It’s the one I recommend as my top pick in WIRED’s guide to the Best Espresso Machines, over other estimable contenders from Breville that include the Barista Touch ($1,000) and the Barista Pro ($850). And it’s the one that best mixes full-flavored, nuanced espresso with the ease of machine-guided, touchscreen operation. It’s versatile, it’s powerful, its PID controller means the brew temperature is quite stable, and it makes absolutely lovely cups—espresso that’s denser and more intensely aromatic than the coffee made by any other machine on this list, whether in bringing out the fruity berry notes in an anaerobic light roast or the dark chocolate of a roasty Italian.

In the finicky, often difficult world of classic home espresso machines, the Oracle Jet is a paragon of simplicity and machine-guided brewing: It’s a miracle that one can so easily pull such delicious and nuanced shots that remain so sensitive to the character of each bean. But that sensitivity still makes the Oracle Jet a little more finicky than other machines on this list. And while the automatic milk frothing is quite good, it’s not as failsafe as our favorites here. (I still like steaming milk manually on the Breville, versus using the auto-froth.).

Which is to say that as a latte machine, this Breville is all about the espresso. If you want espresso that will distill the beauteous character of fresh-roasted beans but still don't want to try overly hard—on a machine whose intuitive touchscreen tutorial will guide you to lovely flat whites and capps? This is your huckleberry.

For those who’d rather not fuss with beans at all but still want a lovely milk-frothed latte and cappuccino in the morning, there is this clever two-piece setup from Nespresso—with “espresso” on one machine via Vertuo coffee pods and an Aeroccino milk frother that’s whisper-quiet and will whip you up some milk foam in a minute. The espresso that comes from pods is not quite espresso, of course, but WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe loved it best of all pod espresso machines, with excellent body and mouthfeel and especially ease. The Vertuo Pop+ will also make a drip-coffee-style mug.

Sources indicate that but this frother bundle generally offers you a good bargain on an all-in-one system, and the Aeroccino is in the upper echelon of milk frothers WIRED has tested. (Note, however, you'll have to plug in each machine separately.) This stated, if you want the ease of pod espresso but are fussy about your milk, you may want to grab a stand-alone Vertuo Pop+ ($129) and the excellent Dreo Baristamaker ($100). Do this when a good sale is running, and you might cobble this together at a similar price to the Aeroccino bundle.

Sources indicate that the Aeroccino was easy to use—pour in your milk of choice and press the button. it will heat and froth your milk automatically—it takes about a minute, and it’s whisper-quiet. Every Nespresso capsule I’ve tried has featured a thick layer of crema, and having whipped, thick milk on top of it made my average cup of coffee a more elevated experience.

Sometimes making a whole latte or cappuccino using an automated machine can be a time suck. Not to mention, sometimes all you really want is frothy milk. That’s where milk frothers come in. These machines beat air into milk, or milk substitutes, to get that nice creamy froth. Former WIRED Reviewer Jaina Grey loved this handheld from Subminimal, a highly specialized immersion blender that makes properly textured, creamy, light, airy, wonderful milk. One screen makes fine-textured milk. One makes “ultra-fine.” Note that Subminimal has also added a milk frothing pitcher called the Nanofoamer Pro ($159) that costs a bit more, but is currently sitting prettily atop our guide to the Best Milk Frothers.

This streamlined machine from relative newcomer Terra Kaffe is a pleasant surprise, given the complexity of Terra Kaffe's first machine, the superautomatic TK-02 (see below), which bristled with features and doohickeys. The Demi is perhaps the dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee. If you don't want to customize your shot, there's just a dial and a button: espresso, lungo, Americano, drip, hot water, bye!

In a recent development, you can click into submenus and edit these to a nerd's content, both by volume and strength. You can adjust among five grinder settings as well—a low but relatively typical number of settings for automatic machines that already grind coarser than espresso machines with portafilters. You may need to futz with grind and dose strength to get good results with light roast, especially on espresso, but with a good medium roast, the Terra Kaffe offers a very smooth ride. Honestly, this is the machine I'd put in a front room for customers to use if I owned a small business. Super easy, no fuss, good for multiple types of people—and the reservoir is major enough at 1.4 liters that you won't be refilling the water all day.

In a recent development, but note that this is actually not a latte machine: It's only half of one. There's no milk frother. Luckily, the world is full of good milk frothing jugs these days, and we especially recommend the Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro ($159), WIRED's favorite milk frother.

Ninja has a habit of taking high-falutin', pro-level, or commercial equipment—whether soft-serve ice cream machines or slushie machines—and finding a way to make it easy, accessible, fun, and probably viral on TikTok. WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane was skeptical about Ninja's first foray into the latte and cappuccino world with the Luxe Cafe Premier (7/10, WIRED Recommends), especially since the machine also promised cold brew and even traditional drip coffee. But she came away impressed.

It has been revealed that this Ninja is not a superautomatic machine like our top automated pick, the Rivelia. It's what the industry likes to call “semiautomatic.” Semiautomatic espresso machines offer a built-in grinder and automatic milk frother but still use a non-pressurized portafilter that will pull a classic espresso shot with full nuance and aromatics. In our espresso maker guide, we recommend the ever-reliable and terrific Breville Barista Express ($700) as WIRED's favorite accessibly priced semiautomatic. But this Ninja is the machine I'd probably give to a beginner, a fresh college grad, or anyone whose first priority is ease and great automatically foamed milk.

The drip coffee is meh, granted. But more than perhaps any semiautomatic machine in its price range, the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier is geared to absolute ease and versatility—with an intuitive digital user interface that helps you along. Depending on your chosen drink, the Ninja Luxe will recommend the appropriate grind size on its display screen and help you dial it in. (This may take a couple of tries.) Milk frothing is easy, and the automatic milk frothing is shockingly good. Plus, you can froth cold foam, for silly cold-foam drinks. See what I mean? Ninja is fun. That stated, we ended up preferring the Luxe Cafe Pro ($750), which costs a little more but adds a welcome auto-tamper and hot water spout.

Amazon (with attached milk carafe).

This superautomatic espresso machine is one of the few coffee machines made by German auto and appliance behemoth Bosch. It is both highly sophisticated and a bit of an odd duck—capable of making an unholy variety of espresso drinks downloaded via firmware. The milk system is especially interesting, and for some, it may be the biggest selling point. On the base model, the milk system is basically a tube you attach to the side of the brew head. You can stick the other end of the tube in any container, and it'll steam whatever milk you've got directly into your cup before adding the espresso. This is great for families who use multiple milks. It's also great for not wasting milk.

The espresso is similar to superautomatics from De'Longhi, which is to say it's a smoother, more rounded, but less nuanced take on espresso that's great for milk drinks. But the “drip” is also interesting. The Bosch 800 “slow brew” coffee—while it does not have the clarity or brightness of drip coffee— is perhaps my favorite drip coffee from an espresso machine, round and roasty and lovely. It extracts only the smooth, chocolate end of the coffee spectrum. I haven't tested the pH, but it seems quite low in acidity. It's nice.

It has been revealed that but here are the caveats: Coffee cup height clearance can be an problem on milk drinks, the pump is a bit louder than some, it's slow to boot up, and some parts feel a bit flimsy or plasticky for a machine in this price range. Also, if you do want an attached milk carafe, it's hundreds of dollars more, depending on current deals.

The delta between home espresso machines and the commercial workhorses used by busy third-wave shops is still thousands of dollars, but that hasn’t stopped both beloved brands and scrappy upstarts from infiltrating the space with more approachable units. Skip the junk and level up to the Casabrews 5700PRO (7/10, WIRED Review), which offers an unfussy take on the art of homemade espresso drinks.

Instead of bewildering noobs with a million settings and onboard tutorials, this 12 x 11 x 16-inch tank of a machine keeps it simple with easily accessible controls for things like temperature and dose volume for extraction, and run time for the onboard grinder. It's a single-boiler machine, not a dual boiler, which means you can’t froth your latte milk at the same time as pulling a shot, but the texture of the frothed milk is perfectly malleable and up to snuff for a basic leaf or rosetta pattern.

In a recent development, the guide rails that hold the portafilter in place are a bit too close to the output spout of the grinder, and temperature controls that deal in absolute rather than relative values would be welcome improvements. But until Casabrews implements our feedback, this is still a solid unit that’s a great pick for anyone who’s ready to never leave their house for a cappuccino ever again. —Pete Cottell.

The superautomatic Terra Kaffe is a pricey hunk of machinery and has its bugs, but considering its ease and customizability, it's worth the price, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane last year. She praised the device's convenience, its ease, the front-facing water filter, waste tray, and milk carafe, and its excellent app (available for iOs and Android) that offers easy controls and the ability to warm up your machine from your bed or the bathroom.

Drinks like latte macchiatos, drips, and iced coffee can all be adjusted to your tastes, and a milk frothing dial allows you to adjust the milk’s texture from foamy to silky. For those who love true, real, drip coffee, that's the biggest selling point for the Terra Kaffe over our top automated picks, the De'Longhi Rivelia and the Ninja Cafe Luxe Premier: The TK-02 offers it. The drip coffee is also good enough that Shane cleared her Chemex pour-over carafe from her counter.

De’Longhi’s Magnifica Start is a no-nonsense superautomatic with a conical burr grinder, four preset recipes at the push of a button, and the ability to brew a smooth and potent espresso, wrote WIRED contributing reviewer Tyler Shane. As with other high-end De'Longhi devices of the moment, the milk frother is truly impressive, offering seriously luxurious frothed milk. Milk-based recipes at the touch of a button are a latte macchiato and a cappuccino, while espresso and Americanos are the espresso-based options. There’s a slot for ground beans and a hopper for whole beans. Figuring out grind size takes a little trial and error, Shane noted, and it's not an overly quiet machine. But the Start is compact and efficient, and priced far lower than our favorite De'Longhi automatic, the Rivelia. This makes the Magnifica Start a solid investment.

According to recent reports, the key here is automation. We wanted to test machines that make you a cup of coffee with a single touch, or as close to that as possible. So the products on this list are all of the automatic and semiautomatic variety. You fill ’em up and they do all the hard work—or most of it, anyway. Nothing here doesn't have a milk frother that does the work by itself.

Setup and cleanup were especially vital, as was durability. The entire point of a device like this is to save time and energy and/or produce a drink of higher quality than can be made without it, so we didn’t recommend any products that didn’t produce tasty espresso and save time.

In May 2026, WIRED’s UK team gathered four fully automatic machines—the Terra Kaffe TK-02 (above), Philips’ Café Aromis 8000 Series, De'Longhi's Eletta Explore, and Jura E8—and made both lattes and espressos for local industry experts to judge. You can read the results and watch the resulting video here. The Reviews team is currently testing the winner of that challenge, Philips Café Aromis 8000, to see how it compares against the top picks in this guide.

According to recent reports, even if you're not making espresso, the first and best thing you can do to dramatically improve your morning coffee is to buy locally roasted beans. Plug your city or region and “locally roasted coffee beans” into Google and you will be glad you did. The reason that your locally roasted coffee will taste worlds better than anything you'd buy from a major coffee roaster (like Starbucks, Illy, or Gevalia) is simple: Good coffee starts to lose flavor the moment it's roasted. Get it fresh and you're giving yourself a much better chance at high-quality espresso.

Want some help finding the best roasters? For some of our favorite mail-order brands, with beans often roasted the same day or week they're placed in the mail, check out our roundup of the Best Coffee Subscription Services.

I hate to break it to you, but pre-ground coffee from a supermarket bag is pretty much always worse. Unless you see a roasting date on the bag, you probably have no idea when the roaster actually roasted it. If the roaster is a French or Italian brand, there's a good chance it was months ago. Coffee is best when it's fresh, ideally brewed a week or two after it's roasted. And grinding the beans dramatically increases the rate at which coffee degrades. This doesn't just affect how the coffee tastes. It affects how well the espresso maker will push water through the beans, leading to possible blowouts or bad extraction.

In a recent development, if you haven’t made espresso before and you don't have access to a coffee grinder, we recommend you buy locally roasted beans. Just ask your local coffee roaster for a fine (espresso) grind. We've tried a lot of pre-ground espresso blends from popular companies like Lavazza, Gevalia, and Café Bustelo. They were all very dark and very bitter, partially because they are all either imported or roasted in major batches and shipped all over the world. Pre-ground coffee will always be a little stale, and it's hard to get a good cup from coffee that's started to degrade—which happens fast after you grind it.

Get it ground fresh from a local roaster, and you'll have about a two-week window before you'll notice any difference. Many of the machines recommended here come with a grinder, so whole beans are already the best choice. But our roundup of The Best Coffee Grinders can also provide some guidance here, if you want to get into the grinding game, buy whole beans, and keep your coffee tasting its best.

It has been revealed that look, milk is milk. Anything that contains milk has the potential to get strange over time, and this includes the milk containers and milk frothers on automatic espresso machines. WIRED's previous espresso reviewer, Jaina Grey, was extremely sensitive to this issue—devoting her time to dishwashering, soaping, scrubbing, and otherwise testing the best methods for making sure that milk containers on automatic espresso machines remain sacrosanct environments.

It has been revealed that regular washing is, of course, the first and best recourse. But occasionally, you'll also want to sterilize your milk reservoir and milk frother.

First, hand-wash it with soap and water as usual, and make sure you get a sponge into those corners. Next up, there are a couple of options. The most effective will be a food-grade sanitizer like Star San, or One Step. Essentially, just make a dilution per the instructions on either product, pour that into a spray bottle, give the inside of the milk container a couple of sprays, and let it dry on a drying rack.

The second-best option, the one that uses things you probably have in your house right now, is a mix of distilled white vinegar and plain old tap water. If you have staining or really stubborn smells, you'll want to let it soak. Try adding about one shot glass (1.5 ounces) of distilled white vinegar and fill the container up the rest of the way with warm water. Let it soak for about 30 minutes, then rinse it out till there's no more vinegar smell, and you should be good to go.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now detects and recovers hung training jobs on Slurm clusters

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports hung job detection for Slurm-orchestrated clusters, which finds training jobs that have stopped making progress and returns them to the job queue.
  • According to recent reports, now, if a training run hangs, HyperPod detects it within minutes from the job's output and GPU activity, or from log patterns that you define, such as your training step message or an NCCL error, and writes an event to Amazon CloudWatch.
  • Hung job detection is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Slurm in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.To learn more, see hung job detection in the user guide and the blog post.

Industry observers note that amazon SageMaker HyperPod now supports hung job detection for Slurm-orchestrated clusters, which finds training jobs that have stopped making progress and returns them to the job queue. SageMaker HyperPod helps you provision resilient clusters for training and deploying AI/ML models. Previously, a job that hung on an NCCL timeout, a stalled data pipeline, or a deadlock kept its GPUs while Slurm reported it as running, until you noticed that the job is not making progress.

According to recent reports, now, if a training run hangs, HyperPod detects it within minutes from the job's output and GPU activity, or from log patterns that you define, such as your training step message or an NCCL error, and writes an event to Amazon CloudWatch. You can also have HyperPod cancel the hung job and let Slurm requeue it, so the job can restart from its last checkpoint instead of holding its GPUs idle. You turn on detection per job with an environment variable that points to a rules file, and it works with any framework, including PyTorch, TensorFlow, and JAX, without changes to your code or containers.

Hung job detection is available for HyperPod clusters orchestrated by Slurm in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available.To learn more, see hung job detection in the user guide and the blog post.

Breaking: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • It has been revealed that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

It has been revealed that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

According to recent reports, we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Recent findings suggest that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

Sources indicate that RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

Industry observers note that this section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Sources indicate that each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

In a recent development, we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

It has been revealed that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

In a recent development, 858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below demonstrates how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

In a recent development, qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

Sources indicate that the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

According to recent reports, the figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below highlights what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which highlighted that 0.1 worked best).

Sources indicate that we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

According to recent reports, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

According to recent reports, the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

It has been revealed that the number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

According to recent reports, we started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each revision below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

It has been revealed that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Recent findings suggest that use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

Recent findings suggest that the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

Sources indicate that we evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Recent findings suggest that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

Sources indicate that all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

Industry observers note that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Sources indicate that results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

Recent findings suggest that this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

According to recent reports, does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

Recent findings suggest that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

According to recent reports, throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Sources indicate that nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.

Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.
  • Recent findings suggest that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away.
  • But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Recent findings suggest that google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

According to recent reports, “There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the massive questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really promptly.”.

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

Industry observers note that the resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.

If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.

So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).

“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” notes Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”.

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.

“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.

But the newly introduced findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

Industry observers note that A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

According to recent reports, the analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla notes. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

Sources indicate that “All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he states. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”.

The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.

Sources indicate that companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google revealed its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the organization Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.

Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other problems are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and  academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.

The latest papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” indicates Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the newly introduced studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but key issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.

“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund mentioned in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.

But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, indicates the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”.

Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Recent findings suggest that yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the latest findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.

Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.

“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he notes.

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod extends AMI auto-patching to Slurm and inference on EKS

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (325 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now automatically patches AMIs on Slurm clusters and introduces a latest AMI patching strategy for Amazon EKS clusters that deploy inference workloads.
  • Now, HyperPod patches both while jobs and models keep running:.
  • According to recent reports, auto-patching (Slurm): HyperPod patches each node only when it is idle, so running jobs aren't disrupted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod now automatically patches AMIs on Slurm clusters and introduces a latest AMI patching strategy for Amazon EKS clusters that deploy inference workloads. SageMaker HyperPod is purpose-built infrastructure for training and deploying foundation models at scale. Previously, patching a Slurm cluster meant waiting for training runs to finish, scheduling downtime, and upgrading nodes by hand, which could take days of coordination between infrastructure admins and research scientists. Also, auto-patching on Amazon EKS waited for nodes to go idle, which suited training workloads but left nodes serving inference workloads, which rarely go idle, without critical AMI updates.

Now, HyperPod patches both while jobs and models keep running:.

According to recent reports, auto-patching (Slurm): HyperPod patches each node only when it is idle, so running jobs aren't disrupted. Teams no longer have to choose between training and security, and can keep clusters secure without coordination between infrastructure admins and research scientists. Each HyperPod AMI has an ImageReleaseVersion that follows semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) across the NVIDIA driver, CUDA, EFA, NCCL, and OS kernel. Auto-patching applies only patch-level updates to the version you select (for example, 1.4.x), so you get security fixes without upgrades that could break your training jobs.

DrainFirst patching strategy (Amazon EKS): HyperPod patches nodes that run inference workloads in rolling batches, draining pods while respecting your Pod Disruption Budgets, so your model keeps serving. If a drain times out, you choose whether HyperPod force-evicts the remaining pods for an urgent patch or skips the node to protect a critical model deployment.

When a patch AMI is released, HyperPod schedules the patch 21 days out and notifies you through AWS Health. You can apply it earlier, defer it up to 60 days measured from the patch AMI release date, or turn it off.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is available. To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker HyperPod AMI automatic patching in the user guide.

Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model.
  • Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a newly introduced looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Recent findings suggest that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

#40570. Amazon CloudFront Introduces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (197 w)

Amazon CloudFront Introduces HTTP/2 Support for Connections to Origins

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (197 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins.
  • Sources indicate that until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection.
  • Recent findings suggest that HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations.

Amazon CloudFront now supports HTTP/2 connections to custom origins and VPC origins. HTTP/2 lets CloudFront send many requests over fewer connections to your origin. This means fewer connections and TLS handshakes for your origin to handle, which improves performance for API and agentic workloads, such as AI agents calling MCP servers or mobile and web apps calling backend APIs.

Sources indicate that until now, CloudFront connected to origins only over HTTP/1.1, which handles one request at a time per connection. When traffic spiked, for example when an AI agent made many tool calls at once, CloudFront had to open more origin connections. Each new connection added latency and load. With HTTP/2, those requests share connections, so your origin does less work and responds faster. HTTP/2 is also supported for WebSocket connections that support extended CONNECT. If your origin doesn't support HTTP/2, CloudFront automatically falls back to HTTP/1.1, so you don't need to change anything on your origin.

Recent findings suggest that HTTP/2 to origins is available from all CloudFront edge locations. There is no additional cost for using HTTP/2 to origins. To learn more, visit Origin HTTP version in the CloudFront Developer Guide.

A newly introduced report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.

Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.

But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.

Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering.

Industry observers note that amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime instances are now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region. Runtime instances run your agents on Amazon EC2 instances in your own account, while AgentCore handles provisioning, patching, scaling, and lifecycle management.

With runtime instances, teams in AWS GovCloud (US) can choose GPU-accelerated, memory-optimized, or compute-optimized instance types for their agents and run agent sessions of up to 14 days. Agent instances, storage volumes, and session data stay in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region, which helps public sector organizations and their partners meet data residency and compliance requirements. Runtime instances work alongside the default serverless, microVM-based AgentCore runtime, so you can pick the right compute for each agent without changing how you deploy or invoke it.

You are charged for the management of the compute provisioned, in addition to your Amazon EC2 costs. To get started, visit AWS News Blog or AgentCore documentation. To learn about pricing, visit AgentCore pricing.
